notes: How fast a pack loses capacity, per pack model rather than per chemistry. Cooling design and cell format drive far more of the spread between real fleets than cathode chemistry does: two NMC packs of the same vintage age quite differently if one is liquid-cooled and the other is not.

fade_at_8y is total capacity lost after eight years by a pack of this model driven at reference_km_per_year in a temperate climate. It already includes the cycling such a car does, which is why cycle_life only applies to the DIFFERENCE between a pack's actual cycle count and that reference. Adding a full cycle term on top would count the same wear twice.

calendar_exponent of 0.5 makes fade go with the square root of time. That is the shape field data shows and the shape SEI growth predicts: a visible drop in the first year, then a long flattening. A straight line fits neither end.

knee_onset_soh and knee_acceleration steepen the curve near the end of life, where lithium plating and lost active material start to compound. The acceleration is deliberately mild: fade_at_8y is calibrated on real packs that were already ageing this way, so a sharp knee on top of it would charge them twice for the same mechanism.

spread_points_at_8y is one standard deviation in state-of-health points at eight years, across packs of the same model and age. It is what makes 'your pack is ageing faster than most' a statement rather than an impression, and it is wide on purpose: real fleets of one model differ by more than most single-number claims admit.

These are cohort central estimates calibrated against published fleet-telemetry studies, OEM warranty floors and aggregated owner-reported capacity readings. They describe a population, never an individual pack. A measured state of health always outranks anything here.
Everything in this file can be overridden from battery-data, where the same figures carry provenance and validity windows. See docs/aging.md.
